questions.title: Adult Ascaris may be found in faeces
questions.question: Ova and Sometimes adult Parasites in faeces are found in?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fasciola hepatica is diagnosed by its egg on stool or duodenal-aspirate examination; the small adult fluke is not a stool finding.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Heterophyes heterophyes is diagnosed by its small egg on stool examination; the tiny adult fluke is not a stool finding.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hymenolepis nana is diagnosed by eggs alone in stool; its small adult worm is not a practical stool finding.
explanations.D: Correct. Ascaris lumbricoides adult worms may themselves be passed in stool or vomited and directly identified, in addition to the more usual egg finding -- the adult worm itself can be a diagnostic finding, unlike Ancylostomiasis, which by contrast is diagnosed in routine practice by finding eggs, since its adult worms remain firmly attached to the intestinal mucosa. The large size of the adult female (up to 20-35 cm) makes it easily recognisable when passed.

questions.learning_objective: State that Ascaris lumbricoides adult worms may occasionally be passed in faeces, alongside ova.

questions.title: Enterobius causes nocturnal enuresis
questions.question: The commonest parasite causing nocturnal enuresis in children is?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ascaris lumbricoides does not classically cause perianal irritation or nocturnal enuresis; its symptoms relate to intestinal bulk or pulmonary migration.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ancylostoma duodenale causes iron-deficiency anaemia and skin (ground itch) symptoms, not nocturnal enuresis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hymenolepis nana causes nonspecific abdominal symptoms in heavy infection, not the perianal-itch-driven nocturnal enuresis classically linked to pinworm.
explanations.D: Correct. Enterobius vermicularis infection classically presents with perianal pruritus and, in children, nocturnal enuresis -- the gravid female's nighttime migration to the perianal skin to lay eggs causes intense itching that disturbs sleep and is the commonest parasitic cause of nocturnal enuresis. This clinical picture is one of the most frequently tested associations for this species.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Enterobius vermicularis as the commonest parasitic cause of nocturnal enuresis in children.

questions.title: Ascaris, hookworm and Strongyloides migrate through the lung
questions.question: The following helminthes have migratory cycle in the lung?

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. It is true Ancylostoma duodenale's larva migrates through the lung, but this is only one of three species sharing the same migratory pattern.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. It is true Ascaris lumbricoides's larva migrates through the lung, but this is only one of three species sharing the same migratory pattern.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone. It is true Strongyloides stercoralis's larva migrates through the lung, but this is only one of three species sharing the same migratory pattern.
explanations.D: Correct. Ascaris lumbricoides, Ancylostoma duodenale and Strongyloides stercoralis larvae all migrate through the lungs as part of their normal life cycle -- gut wall to bloodstream to lung to airway, then swallowed back to the small intestine. This shared pulmonary migratory phase is why acute or heavy infection with any of the three can produce Loeffler's syndrome (chest symptoms and high blood eosinophilia).

questions.learning_objective: State that Ascaris lumbricoides, Ancylostoma duodenale and Strongyloides stercoralis all have a pulmonary larval migratory phase.

questions.title: Trichuris does not inhabit the small intestine
questions.question: The following nematodes inhabit the small intestine EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ancylostoma duodenale inhabits the small intestine, so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ascaris lumbricoides inhabits the small intestine as an adult, so it is not the exception.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Strongyloides stercoralis inhabits the small intestine (its adult female burrows into the mucosa of the duodenum/upper jejunum), so it is not the exception.
explanations.D: Correct. Trichuris trichiura and Enterobius vermicularis both inhabit the large intestine, unlike the small-intestinal Ancylostoma duodenale, Ascaris lumbricoides and Strongyloides stercoralis. Trichuris specifically anchors in the caecum and adjacent large-bowel segments by its thin, whip-like anterior end, making it the exception in this small-intestine-habitat list.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Trichuris trichiura as the exception that does not inhabit the small intestine.

questions.title: Trichuriasis causes rectal prolapse
questions.question: Parasitic infection complicated by rectal prolapse is?

explanations.A: Correct. Rectal prolapse is a recognised complication of heavy Trichuris trichiura infection (trichuriasis) in children -- the sheer worm burden anchored in the rectum and distal colon, combined with straining from associated diarrhoea, can pull the rectal mucosa outward. This complication is a classic clinical association tested for this species.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ascariasis's classic complications are intestinal obstruction, appendicitis and biliary obstruction from bulk worm masses, not rectal prolapse.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ancylostomiasis's classic complication is iron-deficiency anaemia from chronic blood loss, not rectal prolapse.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Strongyloidiasis's classic severe complication is hyperinfection syndrome (especially with corticosteroid use), not rectal prolapse.

questions.learning_objective: Identify trichuriasis as the parasitic infection complicated by rectal prolapse.

questions.title: Ancylostoma infects by skin penetration
questions.question: Infection with Ancylostoma duodenale is through?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ancylostoma duodenale is not acquired by egg ingestion, unlike Ascaris, Trichuris or Enterobius.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ingestion of Cyclops is the transmission route for Dracunculus medinensis, not Ancylostoma duodenale.
explanations.C: Correct. Ground itch is caused by penetration of human skin by the infective filariform larva of Ancylostoma duodenale. This skin-penetration route, from larvae on contaminated soil, is the standard portal of entry for hookworm. It produces an itchy local reaction (ground itch) at the site of penetration before the larva migrates onward through the bloodstream and lungs.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Skin penetration by the filariform larva (option C) is the correct route, so 'none of the above' is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that Ancylostoma duodenale infects man through skin penetration by its filariform larva.

questions.title: Ascaris pneumonitis features dyspnea, cough and eosinophilia
questions.question: Ascaris pneumonitis is characterized by?

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. It is true dyspnea is a feature of Ascaris pneumonitis, but this is only one of three jointly true features offered.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. It is true cough is a feature of Ascaris pneumonitis, but this is only one of three jointly true features offered.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone. It is true eosinophilia is a feature of Ascaris pneumonitis, but this is only one of three jointly true features offered.
explanations.D: Correct. Ascaris pneumonitis (part of Loeffler's syndrome, with chest symptoms and high eosinophilia during pulmonary larval migration) is characterised by dyspnea, cough and eosinophilia together, all three jointly true. This same pulmonary migratory pattern, and its resulting Loeffler-type picture, is shared by hookworm and Strongyloides as well.

questions.learning_objective: State that Ascaris pneumonitis is characterised by dyspnea, cough and eosinophilia.

questions.title: Trichuris trichiura inhabits the caecum
questions.question: Trichuris trichiura?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pin worm is the common name for Enterobius vermicularis, not Trichuris trichiura, whose own common name is whip worm.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Trichuris trichiura has no larval migratory phase outside the intestine, unlike Ascaris, hookworm or Strongyloides.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Trichuris trichiura eggs are passed immature (unembryonated), not mature, requiring further development in soil before becoming infective.
explanations.D: Correct. Trichuris trichiura is a whip-like worm with an oviparous female that anchors in the caecum by its attenuated end, and has no migratory phase outside the intestine. This caecum-and-adjacent-large-bowel habitat, together with its lack of a migratory phase, is the correct description among the four options.

questions.learning_objective: State that Trichuris trichiura inhabits the caecum and adjacent large-bowel segments, with no migratory phase.

questions.title: Cutaneous larva migrans is caused by Ancylostoma caninum
questions.question: Cutaneous larva migrans resulting from exposure to the following parasite?

explanations.A: Correct. Cutaneous larva migrans is an itchy, serpiginous, slowly advancing red track in the skin caused by an animal hookworm larva (classically Ancylostoma braziliense or A. caninum, dog/cat hookworms) that cannot penetrate past the human dermis. Because these larvae are adapted to a non-human host, they lack the enzymes to cross the dermal basement membrane and instead wander only within the epidermis, producing the visible track.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ancylostoma duodenale is the human hookworm; its larva completes a normal human infection (penetrating to the bloodstream and lungs) rather than wandering harmlessly in the skin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Necator americanus is the other human hookworm; like A. duodenale, its larva completes normal human infection rather than causing cutaneous larva migrans.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ancylostoma caninum (option A) is the correct cause, so 'none of the above' is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Ancylostoma caninum (an animal hookworm) as the classic cause of cutaneous larva migrans.

questions.title: Strongyloides infects by skin penetration
questions.question: Strongyloides stercoralis infects man through?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Strongyloides stercoralis is not acquired by egg ingestion; it does not even pass an infective egg to the environment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The filariform larva is the infective stage, but it infects by skin penetration, not by being ingested.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The rhabditiform larva is a non-infective, developmental stage; it is the filariform larva that penetrates skin.
explanations.D: Correct. The usual portal of entry of Strongyloides stercoralis into the human body is the skin, penetrated by its infective filariform larva. This is the same skin-penetration mechanism used by Ancylostoma duodenale. Strongyloides's filariform larva is nonetheless unsheathed and notch-tailed, unlike hookworm's sheathed larva.

questions.learning_objective: State that Strongyloides stercoralis infects man by skin penetration of its filariform larva.

questions.title: Strongyloides larva develops to adult under favourable soil conditions
questions.question: Strongyloides stercoralis larva changes to adult when?

explanations.A: Correct. The life cycle of Strongyloides stercoralis can proceed by a direct cycle, an indirect (free-living) cycle, or internal autoinfection; under favourable soil conditions (adequate warmth and moisture), rhabditiform larvae shed in stool can develop into free-living adult males and females in soil, completing an entire generation outside the human host. This free-living generation is a feature unique to Strongyloides among the nematodes in this chapter.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Under unfavourable soil conditions, rhabditiform larvae instead moult directly into infective filariform larvae (the direct cycle) rather than developing into free-living adults.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Unsuitable temperature is one form of unfavourable condition, which instead favours direct development to the infective filariform larva, not to a free-living adult.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Favourable soil conditions (option A) is the correct answer, so 'none of the above' is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that Strongyloides stercoralis larvae develop into free-living adults under favourable soil conditions.

questions.title: Strongyloides alone migrates outside the human body
questions.question: Parasite migration outside the body occurs in?

explanations.A: Correct. The life cycle of Strongyloides stercoralis can proceed by a direct cycle, an indirect (free-living) cycle, or internal autoinfection. Its free-living (indirect) cycle allows an entire generation of free-living adult worms to develop and reproduce in soil, independent of a human host. This pattern of development and migration outside the body is not shared by Ancylostoma duodenale, Trichostrongylus colubriformis or Trichuris trichiura.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ancylostoma duodenale's larvae develop through free-living larval stages in soil, but the species has no free-living adult generation reproducing outside a host, unlike Strongyloides.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Trichostrongylus colubriformis's larvae develop in soil/vegetation to the infective stage, but it has no free-living adult generation reproducing outside a host, unlike Strongyloides.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Trichuris trichiura's eggs mature in soil, but it has no free-living adult generation reproducing outside a host, unlike Strongyloides.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Strongyloides stercoralis as uniquely capable of a free-living generation outside the human body.

questions.title: Capillaria philippinensis is acquired from undercooked fish
questions.question: Man gets infected with Capillaria Philippinensis when eating?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Undercooked pork is the source of Trichinella spiralis, not Capillaria philippinensis.
explanations.B: Correct. Capillaria philippinensis is acquired by eating insufficiently cooked fish, not by improperly washed vegetables, and causes watery diarrhoea diagnosed by its egg. Freshwater fish serve as the intermediate host carrying the infective larval stage. This is why undercooked fish, not another food source, is the specific transmission route tested for this species.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Undercooked beef is the source of Taenia saginata, not Capillaria philippinensis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Eating infected liver is associated with spurious (false) Fasciola infection, not Capillaria philippinensis.

questions.learning_objective: State that Capillaria philippinensis is acquired by eating undercooked fish.

questions.title: Culex is the vector of Wuchereria bancrofti
questions.question: The vector of Wuchereria bancrofti is?

explanations.A: Correct. Bancroftian filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti) is transmitted by the Culex mosquito, adult worms live in the lymphatics, and chronic lymphatic obstruction and fibrosis from dead worms produces elephantiasis. Culex, a culicine mosquito, is the standard vector taught for this species, distinguishing it from the vectors of other filariae tested in this chapter.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Simulium (the blackfly) is the vector of Onchocerca volvulus, not Wuchereria bancrofti.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mansonia is a vector for Brugia malayi in some regions, not the standard vector taught for Wuchereria bancrofti.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chrysops (the deer fly) is the vector of Loa loa, not Wuchereria bancrofti.

questions.learning_objective: State that Culex is the mosquito vector of Wuchereria bancrofti.

questions.title: Adult W. bancrofti worms live in lymph nodes
questions.question: The adult worms of Wuchereria bancrofti are found in?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Blood carries the circulating microfilariae, not the adult worms, which instead reside in the lymphatics.
explanations.B: Correct. Bancroftian filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti) is transmitted by the Culex mosquito, adult worms live in the lymphatics, and chronic lymphatic obstruction and fibrosis from dead worms produces elephantiasis. Adult worms reside in the lymphatic vessels and nodes, mainly of the lower limbs and genital organs, where their presence (living or dying) triggers the inflammatory and, eventually, obstructive changes underlying the disease's clinical picture.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Subcutaneous tissue is instead the habitat of the adult Dracunculus medinensis and Onchocerca volvulus, not Wuchereria bancrofti.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Muscle is instead the site where Trichinella spiralis larvae encyst, not where adult Wuchereria bancrofti worms are found.

questions.learning_objective: State that adult Wuchereria bancrofti worms live in the lymphatics.

questions.title: Culex transmits W. bancrofti cyclodevelopmentally
questions.question: Mode of transmission of Wuchereria bancrofti by female culex?

explanations.A: Correct. Culex transmits Wuchereria bancrofti cyclodevelopmentally: the ingested microfilaria develops through successive larval stages (L1 to L3) within the mosquito to reach the infective filariform larva, but does not multiply in number along the way -- one ingested microfilaria yields, at most, one infective larva. This distinguishes cyclodevelopmental transmission from cyclopropagative transmission, in which the organism both develops and multiplies within the vector.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cyclopropagative transmission (development plus multiplication in the vector) describes organisms such as the malaria parasite in Anopheles, not the filarial larva in Culex, which develops without multiplying.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mechanical transmission (no development within the vector, simple physical carriage) does not apply to filariasis, which requires larval development inside the mosquito.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Transovarian transmission (passage of the organism to the vector's own offspring via the egg) is not how Wuchereria bancrofti is transmitted by Culex.

questions.learning_objective: State that Culex transmits Wuchereria bancrofti cyclodevelopmentally.
